Data structures that work by storing data in a single array have many
advantages and limitations in common:
\index{arrays}%

content: \item Arrays offer constant time access to any value in the array. This is what allows \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{get}(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}})}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{set}(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}},\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} to run in constant time. \item Arrays are not very dynamic. Adding or removing an element near the middle of a list means that a large number of elements in the array need to be shifted to make room for the newly added element or to fill in the gap created by the deleted element. This is why the operations \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}},\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{remove}(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}})}} have running times that depend on \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}. \item Arrays cannot expand or shrink. When the number of elements in the data structure exceeds the size of the backing array, a new array needs to be allocated and the data from the old array needs to be copied into the new array. This is an expensive operation.

We will see that, if carefully managed, the cost of growing and shrinking the backing array does not add much to the cost of an \emph{average} operation. content: \seclabel{arraystack} \index{ArrayStack@ArrayStack} An ArrayStack implements the list interface using an array \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{a}}}}, called the \emph{backing array}. The list element with index \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}} is stored in \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{a}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}]}}. At most times, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{a}}}} is larger than strictly necessary, so an integer \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}} is used to keep track of the number of elements actually stored in \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{a}}}}. In this way, the list elements are stored in \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{a}}[0]}},\ldots,\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{a}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}-1]}} and, at all times, $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{length}(\ensuremath{\mathit{a}})}} \ge \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}$.

content: The operations of adding and removing elements from an ArrayStack are illustrated in \figref{arraystack}. To implement the \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}},\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} operation, we first check if \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{a}}}} is already full. If so, we call the method \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{resize}()}} to increase the size of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{a}}}}. How \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{resize}()}} is implemented will be discussed later. For now, it is sufficient to know that, after a call to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{resize}()}}, we can be sure that $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{length}(\ensuremath{\mathit{a}})}} > \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}$. With this out of the way, we now shift the elements $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{a}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}]}},\ldots,\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{a}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}-1]}}$ right by one position to make room for \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}, set \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{a}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}]}} equal to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}, and increment \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}.

Implementing the \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{remove}(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}})}} operation is similar. If so, then we call \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{resize}()}} to reduce the size of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{a}}}}.

content: We will show that any time \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{resize}()}} is called, the number of calls to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{add}}}} or \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{remove}}}} since the last call to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{resize}()}} is at least $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}/2-1$. Therefore, if $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}_i$ denotes the value of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}} during the $i$th call to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{resize}()}} and $r$ denotes the number of calls to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{resize}()}}, then the total number of calls to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}},\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} or \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{remove}(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}})}} is at least \[ \sum_{i=1}^{r} (\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}_i/2-1) \le m \enspace , \] which is equivalent to \[ \sum_{i=1}^{r} \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}_i \le 2m + 2r \enspace . \] On the other hand, the total time spent during all calls to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{resize}()}} is \[ \sum_{i=1}^{r} O(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}_i) \le O(m+r) = O(m) \enspace , \] since $r$ is not more than $m$. All that remains is to show that the number of calls to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}},\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} or \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{remove}(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}})}} between the $(i-1)$th and the $i$th call to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{resize}()}} is at least $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}_i/2$. There are two cases to consider. In the first case, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{resize}()}} is being called by \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}},\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} because the backing array \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{a}}}} is full, i.e., $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{length}(\ensuremath{\mathit{a}})}} = \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}=\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}_i$. Consider the previous call to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{resize}()}}: after this previous call, the size of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{a}}}} was \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{length}(\ensuremath{\mathit{a}})}}, but the number of elements stored in \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{a}}}} was at most $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{length}(\ensuremath{\mathit{a}})}}/2=\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}_i/2$. But now the number of elements stored in \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{a}}}} is $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}_i=\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{length}(\ensuremath{\mathit{a}})}}$, so there must have been at least $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}_i/2$ calls to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}},\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} since the previous call to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{resize}()}}. The second case occurs when \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{resize}()}} is being called by \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{remove}(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}})}} because $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{length}(\ensuremath{\mathit{a}})}} \ge 3\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}=3\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}_i$. Therefore, the number of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{remove}(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}})}} operations since the last call to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{resize}()}} is at least \begin{align*} R & \ge \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{length}(\ensuremath{\mathit{a}})}}/2 - 1 - \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{length}(\ensuremath{\mathit{a}})}}/3 \\ & = \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{length}(\ensuremath{\mathit{a}})}}/6 - 1 \\ & = (\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{length}(\ensuremath{\mathit{a}})}}/3)/2 - 1 \\ & \ge \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}_i/2 -1\enspace . \end{align*} In either case, the number of calls to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}},\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} or \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{remove}(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}})}} that occur between the $(i-1)$th call to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{resize}()}} and the $i$th call to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{resize}()}} is at least $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}_i/2-1$, as required to complete the proof.

Although the asymptotic performance of the DualArrayDeque is no better than that of the ArrayDeque, it is still worth studying, since it offers a good example of how to make a sophisticated data structure by combining two simpler data structures. A DualArrayDeque represents a list using two ArrayStacks. Recall that an ArrayStack is fast when the operations on it modify elements near the end. A DualArrayDeque places two ArrayStacks, called \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{front}}}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{back}}}}, back-to-back so that operations are fast at either end.

content: We will show that, if \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{balance}()}} is forced to shift elements, then the number of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}},\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{remove}(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}})}} operations since the last time any elements were shifted by \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{balance}()}} is at least $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}/2-1$. As in the proof of \lemref{arraystack-amortized}, this is sufficient to prove that the total time spent by \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{balance}()}} is $O(m)$. content: Most of the data structures described in this chapter are folklore. They can be found in implementations dating back over 30 years. For example, implementations of stacks, queues, and deques, which generalize easily to the ArrayStack, ArrayQueue and ArrayDeque structures described here, are discussed by Knuth \cite[Section~2.2.2]{k97v1}. Brodnik \etal\ \cite{bcdms99} seem to have been the first to describe the RootishArrayStack and prove a $\sqrt{n}$ lower-bound like that in \secref{rootishspaceusage}. They also present a different structure that uses a more sophisticated choice of block sizes in order to avoid computing square roots in the \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{i2b}(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}})}} method. Within their scheme, the block containing \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}} is block $\lfloor\log (\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}+1)\rfloor$, which is simply the index of the leading 1 bit in the binary representation of $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}+1$. Some computer architectures provide an instruction for computing the index of the leading 1-bit in an integer.
